title: What sampling is, and what it is not
short: A sample is a piece of an existing recording placed inside a new one. Play the same part again with your own hands and it becomes an interpolation; re-record the whole song and it is a cover; rework the original recording and it is a remix. The distinctions sound fussy until money is involved, because each one calls on a different set of owners.

title: Where sampling came from
short: Nobody invented sampling in one go. Composers were cutting up recordings in Paris in 1948, Jamaican engineers were remixing them by 1970, and Bronx DJs were looping drum breaks by hand in 1973, all before a machine existed to do it. The digital sampler arrived in 1979, got cheap by 1987, and produced about four years of dense collage that ended in lawyers' offices. What came after was slower, costlier and spread across the world.

title: The machines
short: A sampler is a digital recorder you can play like an instrument: it measures a sound thousands of times a second, stores the numbers and reads them back at whatever pitch you ask for. The first commercial one, the Fairlight CMI of 1979, was an 8-bit computer with a light pen and a five-figure price in pounds. Eight years later a drum box with 10 seconds of 12-bit memory was setting the sound of hip-hop, and its flaws were kept on purpose when its designer reissued it in 2021.

title: The breaks everyone uses
short: The same few dozen records turn up under other people's songs again and again, and the most used of them is about six seconds of drumming from a 1969 B-side. WhoSampled, a volunteer-built database, listed "Amen, Brother" 6,873 times as of July 2025. The drummer who played it died in 2006 without a royalty, and most of the players behind the other famous breaks tell a similar story.

title: How a flip gets made
short: A flip starts with a find - a record nobody else has, or a new idea about one everybody has - and ends with that sound doing a job its makers never planned. In between, the producer loops, chops, filters, re-pitches, stretches and layers it, and most of those moves began as workarounds for machines with a few seconds of memory. Since about 2018, software has been able to pull the voice, drums or bass back out of a finished mix, which changes what there is to find.

title: Is sampling legal? The law, case by case
short: Every recording carries two copyrights, the song and the performance of it, and a sample touches both, which is why it needs two permissions where a replay needs one. In the US, two federal appeals courts disagree about whether a sliver of a recording can be too small to count, and fair use has saved a sample-type use about once. In the EU, the Kraftwerk case has been in court since 1999 and produced a new definition of pastiche in April 2026. No country has a six-second rule.

title: How to clear a sample
short: A sample needs two yeses, one from whoever owns the recording and one from whoever owns the song, and there is no rate card or central office for either. Each owner names a price - usually a fee up front plus a share of the new track - and any of them is free to say no. Clearing after release is the expensive way round. Re-recording the part instead of lifting it drops the recording owner from the deal, by the US Copyright Office's account, and since about 2021 the companies that own old songs have been pitching that route themselves.

title: Who gets paid
short: Sample money follows paperwork. It goes to whoever owns the recording and whoever owns the song, which is often a label, a publisher or a fund that bought the catalog, and often not the musician you can hear. The drummer on the Amen break never received a royalty for it. A newer economy sells sounds that are cleared in advance - Splice, Tracklib, composer libraries - and each comes with fine print about what "royalty-free" covers.

title: Sampling around the world
short: Every scene samples its own way. Boom bap chopped drums off vinyl, the West Coast hired players to replay funk, French producers ran disco through a filter, jungle built a genre on a few seconds of a 1969 drum solo, and a 1989 Jamaican riddim sits under most of reggaeton and was still before a US federal court in September 2026. Three questions follow the practice everywhere: who is credited, who is paid, and whether a rhythm can be owned at all.

title: AI, stems and what comes next
short: The AI tool most producers use is the one that takes records apart. Song generators are a minority habit, but one generated track, "BBL Drizzy," was sampled on a Drake record in 2024 and cleared by paying only the human who wrote the words. The major labels sued the two biggest generators in 2024; three of those disputes settled into licensing deals in late 2025, and in 2026 the holdouts filed second, far larger suits. As of November 2026 no US court had ruled on whether training a music model on recordings is fair use.

title: Test yourself, and where to dig next
short: Quiz yourself on the breaks, the machines and the case law, learn the trade's vocabulary, run the timeline from tape splices to stem splitters, then go to the best books, films and databases on the subject.
